# On the Uselessness of Poetry

To my mind, poetry is nothing more than a hobby, no different from running model trains around a track or breeding pigeons in a backyard loft. Some men amuse themselves in these ways of an evening, and that is all well and good—but let us not pretend such pastimes constitute real work. Scribbling verses belongs in precisely the same category: a harmless diversion, perhaps, but hardly a serious occupation for any grown man.

Consider what poetry actually produces. It builds nothing you can hold in your hands. It shifts no earth, raises no walls, and manufactures no goods. It earns not a penny in honest trade. And what does it amount to in the end? A clever arrangement of words that could just as easily be turned to selling soap. If your fine phrases are good for anything at all, they are good for advertising—and if they cannot even manage that, then they are good for nothing whatsoever.

So do not come to me asking for twelve pounds a week. I could not defend such a sum to anyone with sense. Think of the bus conductor, out in all weathers, working every hour God sends for a fraction of what you propose to be paid for daydreaming. How could I look that man in the eye and tell him a poet deserves more? It would be indefensible, plain and simple.

I speak, mind you, from a position of some authority. I am an accountant, and a well-paid one. I have a company car and an expense account, and men who answer to me and do as I say. I have earned my standing through discipline and useful labour. What have you earned? What do you command? You produce nothing, you direct nothing, and you contribute nothing that a sensible man could measure.

And let me say one thing more about your sort. Poets, in my experience, are a bad lot through and through—Reds and radicals, addicts and delinquents, the whole immoral crew of them. The stuff they write is rot, every worthless line of it. Take my advice and put such nonsense aside. Go and find yourself some real work, and make something of your life while you still can.

# The Accountant's Reckoning

The poem unfolds as a dramatic monologue delivered by a self-satisfied accountant, a man who measures all things by their monetary value. When a poet approaches him seeking fair compensation for creative work, the accountant responds not with respect but with barely concealed contempt. His voice, dripping with condescension, becomes the vehicle through which the poem mounts its critique of a society that has forgotten how to value art.

The accountant cannot fathom why anyone should pay for verses. To his mind, poetry produces nothing tangible, generates no profit, and contributes nothing to the ledgers by which he understands human worth. He contrasts the poet's labor with what he considers "real" work—the honest toil of clerks, merchants, and tradesmen who earn their keep through practical enterprise. In his estimation, the poet is little more than an idle dreamer, someone who has failed to grasp the fundamental economics of respectable life.

Through this satirical portrait, the poem exposes the poverty of philistine values. The accountant regards creative work as fundamentally worthless because it cannot be weighed, sold, or entered into a balance sheet. Worse still, he views poetry with suspicion—as something faintly unhealthy, perhaps even morally corrupting. To him, the poet's preoccupation with beauty and truth represents a kind of dissipation, a wasteful indulgence in matters that serious, productive citizens have long outgrown.

Yet the poem's irony works against the speaker at every turn. The very smugness of the accountant's dismissals reveals the narrowness of his vision. By allowing this materialistic voice to condemn poetry so thoroughly, the poem invites readers to recognize what such a worldview cannot see: that artistic labor demands genuine effort, discipline, and integrity, and that its value cannot be reduced to commercial terms.

At its heart, the poem dramatizes the enduring tension between commercial worth and artistic integrity. The accountant speaks for a culture that equates value with profit and treats the immeasurable as meaningless. Against this stands the implicit dignity of the poet's craft—a form of work that enriches human life precisely because it refuses the logic of the marketplace. In giving the philistine his say, the poem ultimately reveals how much such thinking impoverishes us all.

# On Poetry, Shaw, and You

Poetry has always occupied a peculiar space in human expression—a form that distills emotion, thought, and observation into carefully chosen words. It speaks to something universal while remaining deeply personal, which is perhaps why it continues to resonate across generations.

## The Wisdom of Shaw

George Bernard Shaw, the celebrated Irish playwright and critic, understood the power of language better than most. Though known primarily for his plays and sharp wit, Shaw appreciated how words could challenge, provoke, and inspire. He once remarked, "Life isn't about finding yourself. Life is about creating yourself." This sentiment captures the same creative spirit that drives poets to craft meaning from the raw material of experience.

Shaw believed in the transformative power of ideas. His work often pushed readers and audiences to question social conventions and examine their own assumptions. In this way, he shared a kinship with poets throughout history—both seek to awaken something in their audience, to make the familiar strange and the strange familiar.

## Where You Come In

But here is the essential truth: poetry means nothing without *you*—the reader. A poem sits silent on the page until your eyes bring it to life. Your experiences, memories, and emotions complete the work. The poet provides the words, but you supply the meaning.

When you read a line that stops you cold, that recognition is a collaboration. Shaw understood that art requires participation, that the audience is never passive. You are not merely receiving the poem; you are helping to create it anew each time you engage with it.

## A Living Conversation

Consider poetry, then, as an ongoing conversation—between writers like Shaw who shaped how we think about language and expression, and you, the reader who breathes new life into every verse. This dynamic relationship ensures that poetry remains vital, relevant, and profoundly human.

So the next time you encounter a poem, remember: you are an essential part of its existence. The words may belong to the poet, but the experience belongs entirely to you.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dramatic monologue from the perspective of a hard-nosed accountant dismissing poetry as a worthless hobby and telling the poet to get a real job.
counterfactuals.output:
**"The Bottom Line"**

Sit down. No—don't recite. I've heard enough of your *couplets* to last a fiscal year.

You come in here, twenty-nine years old, with holes in your shoes and a notebook full of—what? Feelings? You know what I've got a notebook full of? Numbers. And numbers, my friend, do not *rhyme*. They do not *weep*. They do not stand in the rain being "moved" by the color of a leaf. They *balance*. Or they don't. And when they don't, someone pays.

You think I don't feel things? I feel the mortgage. I feel the deadline. I feel the exquisite, throbbing poetry of a spreadsheet that reconciles to the penny. There's a music in that too—you just can't hear it over the sound of your own sighing.

Let me tell you about the sonnet you sent your mother instead of a check.

She framed it. That's lovely. You can't eat a frame. You can't heat a house with fourteen lines about her hands. Her hands, incidentally, are chapped because she's still working double shifts to fund your—what do we call it—your *art*.

I've done the arithmetic on your life, because clearly nobody else will. Forty poems published. Total earnings? Enough for a sandwich. Time invested? Fifteen years. That, in my profession, is called a *loss*. A sustained, catastrophic, unrecoverable loss. If you were a company, I'd have folded you. If you were an asset, I'd have written you off.

Get a job. A *real* one. One with a desk and a name-tag and a pension that doesn't require the muse to show up. Wear the tie. Learn the software. Watch the little numbers march into their little columns, obedient, honest, *there*—

—not like your metaphors, which promise everything and deliver nothing you can bank.

You want beauty? Compound interest. That's beauty. That's a poem that pays you back.

Now.

Close the notebook. Take the folder. There's an opening in accounts payable, and I—

*(a pause; he glances, despite himself, at a poem left on the desk)*

...You left this here.

"The ledger of my father's silence." Hm.

...It doesn't balance. There's a word missing in the third line—you'd want *"weight,"* not *"wait,"* unless—

*(he stops, catches himself)*

—unless you meant both.

Take the folder.

Accounts payable. Monday. Eight sharp.

And leave the poem. I'll—

I'll shred it later.
